interactions.summary: The reading enters the giant circle: Dante mistakes giants for towers, Virgil explains the error, Nimrod howls in Babel gibberish, Iphialtes is chained for rebelling against Jove, and Antaeus is named as the speaking giant who can lower the travelers further down.
interactions.speaker_attribution: Student reading Dante aloud with one Jiang gloss

claims.claim: The canto stages an interpretive mistake in which distance makes giants look like city towers until Virgil corrects Dante's faulty image.
The reading presents giants as creatures whose combination of acute intelligence, evil will, and massive power makes ordinary human defense impossible.
Jiang glosses Nimrod as the builder of the Tower of Babel and says his punishment is incomprehensible speech.
The reading distinguishes chained rebel giants like Iphialtes from Antaeus, who is unchained and able to carry Dante and Virgil down toward Cocytus.

signature_moments.moment: As the fog thins, what looked like a fortified city resolves into giants, so clearer sight increases terror rather than calming it.
signature_moments.source_phrase: my error fled from me my terror grew
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It preserves the canto's movement from mistaken image to overwhelming reality.

signature_moments.moment: Nimrod's punishment is linguistic ruin itself: the Babel-builder now speaks a tongue no one can understand, and no one can understand him in return.
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It turns failed world-building into failed communication.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: The Babel-builder giant whose punishment is incomprehensible speech, making him a figure of failed linguistic empire.
